title: HCI — Multiple Window Strategies, Tightly Coupled Windows, Personal Role Manager, Elastic Windows
description: Exam revision: origins of windowing, ten multiple-window strategies, coordination by tightly coupled windows, overview + detail image browsing, personal role management and elastic windows.
endCard: 📘 Multiple-Window Design — revised. You've got this!

scenes.title: Intro

viz.s: How do you see many things at once on one screen?

lines: Your task needs an email, a document, and a chart, all at once. How should a screen show them?
That's the problem of multiple window design.
We'll cover where windows came from, ten layout strategies, tightly coupled windows, image browsing, the personal role manager, and elastic windows.

scenes.title: 1. Where windows came from

nodes.b: printed output on an ever-growing scroll of paper
displays let users scroll back through the session
users need to jump to related text or graphics
8010 Star + Smalltalk → multiple windows = multiple views on a large, high-res screen

lines: Early computers used a teletype, printing output on an ever-growing scroll of paper.
When designers switched to displays, electronic scrolling let users go back through the session. Useful,
but designers saw similar situations where users had to jump around to related text or graphics.

The multiple window strategy evolved at Xerox PARC, with the eighty ten Star system and the Smalltalk programming system. On a large, high resolution screen, windows give multiple views that make a task easier.

scenes.title: 2. Strategies — part 1

kinds.n: Fixed number, size, place · space-filling tiling
Variable size, place, number · space-filling tiling

lines: The challenge of giving access to multiple sources of information has stimulated many solutions.
Multiple monitors: more than one monitor used for display.
Split displays: more than one window shown at once, like in WordPerfect five.
Rapid display flipping: switching quickly between full views.
Fixed number, size and place, with space filling tiling.
Variable size, place and number, still space filling tiling.
And non space filling tiling, where tiles don't cover the whole screen.

scenes.title: 3. Strategies — part 2

viz.name: winlayouts
viz.note: 10 strategies: Monitors · Split · Flip · Fixed tile · Variable tile · Non-filling · Piles · Zoom · Overlap · Cascade

lines: Piles of tiles: windows stacked in groups, like taskbar icons stacked when more than one window is open.
Window zooming: a window grows to fill the screen, then shrinks back.
Arbitrary overlaps: windows placed anywhere, overlapping freely.
And cascades: windows stacked diagonally so every title bar stays visible.
That's all ten strategies.

scenes.title: 4. Coordination by tightly coupled windows

nodes.b: task concept — how information objects change based on user actions
interface concept that supports coordination among windows
study tasks → task-specific coordinations; developers also support generic ones

lines: Coordination is a task concept: it describes how information objects change based on user actions.
Tight coupling among windows is the interface concept that supports coordination.
A careful study of user tasks can lead to task specific coordinations, based on sequences of actions. There are also generic coordinations that interface developers can support.

scenes.title: 5. Seven generic coordinations

items.b: scroll one window, the other scrolls with it
pick a node in a tree, its contents show in another window
select an item / tool, a detail window appears
2D overview + detail view (e.g. charts)
opening one opens its related windows
closing one closes its dependents
restore the whole arrangement later

viz.note: Sync · Hierarchy · Direct · 2-D · Open · Close · Save

lines: Seven generic coordinations. Synchronized scrolling: scroll one window, and the coupled one scrolls too.
Hierarchical browsing: select a node in a tree, and its contents appear in another window.
Direct selection: select an item or tool, and its detail appears.
Two dimensional browsing: a two D overview coupled to a detail view.
Dependent windows opening, and dependent windows closing, where related windows open and close together.
And save or open window state, to restore the whole arrangement later.
Sync, hierarchy, direct, two D, open, close, save.

scenes.title: 6. Image browsing — overview + detail
lines: When browsing large images, from medical, geographic, or graphic design systems, a pair of scroll bars is adequate if the image is less than three to five times the screen size.
For larger images, a tight coupling between an overview and a detail view beats single zooming, or several independent windows.
Move the field of view box on the overview, and the detail updates. Pan in the detail, and the box moves in the overview.
Well designed coupled windows have matching aspect ratios in the field of view box and the detail view. Change the shape of either, and the other changes too.
The magnification from overview to detail is the zoom factor. Between five and thirty works well. Beyond that, add an intermediate view.

scenes.title: 7. Zoom factor, layout & fisheye

items.b:
magnification overview → detail
5 – 30: overview + detail pair works
> 30: add an intermediate view
the most common layout — see the big picture and the details at the same time
show detail and overview without obscuring anything — magnify the focus, compress the context

lines: Recap the zoom factor: between five and thirty, a tightly coupled overview and detail pair is effective. Larger, and you need an intermediate view.
Side by side placement of overview and detail is the most common layout, since users see the big picture and details at once.
And attempts to show detail and overview without obscuring anything motivated interest in fisheye views.

scenes.title: 8. Image-browser tasks

items.b: moving focus · comparing · traversing · marking locations to return to later

lines: The design of image browsers should be governed by the user's tasks. These are classified into:
image generation, open-ended exploration, diagnostic,
navigation, and monitoring.
Within these high level tasks, users carry out many low level actions: moving focus, comparing, traversing, or marking locations to return to later.
Memory hook: I Often Draw New Maps.

scenes.title: 9. Toward role-centred design

nodes.b: applications as icons, documents in folders
documents become important, applications fade into the background
next generation — emphasises the user's tasks, not documents

lines: Current GUIs offer a desktop, with applications as icons and documents organised into folders.
A documentary design makes documents more important, and applications fade into the background.
To reach the next generation of user interfaces, the natural progression is role centred design, which emphasises the user's tasks rather than documents.

scenes.title: 10. Personal Role Manager (PRM)

items.b: improves performance, reduces distraction within a role, eases shifting attention between roles
each role has one, set by the user or manager
managing multiple projects with many participants + interviews with 15 experienced users
info organised by the roles a person has in an organisation
remind users of goals, related people, required tasks, scheduled events
all roles visible; current focus occupies most of the screen

lines: A personal role manager, instead of a window manager, could improve performance and reduce distraction while working in a role, and make it easier to shift attention between roles.
In a personal role manager, each role has a vision statement, established by the user or manager.
It was stimulated by experience managing multiple projects with many participants, plus observations and interviews with fifteen experienced users.
The key is organising information according to the roles an individual has in an organisation.
While working in a role, the most relevant information is visible, and these visual cues remind users of their goals, related people, required tasks, and scheduled events.
Screen management is a key function. All roles should be visible, but the current focus of attention can occupy most of the screen.

scenes.title: 11. Task subjects of a role

letters.d: who you work with in the role

lines: The task subjects in a personal role manager are:
a vision statement, a set of people, a task hierarchy, and a schedule.
Memory hook: Very Productive Team Schedule.

scenes.title: 12. Requirements for personal role management

items.b: organise info by users' roles
that matches tasks
fast arrangement of information
find info by nominal, spatial, temporal, visual attributes & relationships
and resumption among roles
for task-domain actions, not interface-domain actions
used productively for tasks

lines: Seven requirements for personal role management. Support a unified framework for organising information according to users' roles.
Provide a visual, spatial layout that matches tasks.
Support multi-window actions for fast arrangement of information.
Support information access with partial knowledge of its nominal, spatial, temporal and visual attributes, and relationships to other information.
Allow fast switching and resumption among roles.
Free the user's cognitive resources to work on task domain actions, rather than interface domain actions.
And use screen space efficiently and productively for tasks.

scenes.title: 13. Elastic windows
lines: Elastic windows organise windows in a space filling, hierarchically nested, tiled layout, designed to support the personal role manager's requirements.
Users change the layout quickly by applying operations to groups of windows.
Elastic resizing enlarges one window, or a group, while shrinking the others in the group,
so users can easily focus on information in different windows.

scenes.title: Recap

viz.s: Many views · coupled windows · roles, not documents
chips: Sync · Hierarchy · Direct · 2D · Open · Close · Save

lines: Quick recap.
Windows began at Xerox PARC. Ten layout strategies, seven generic coordinations, and overview plus detail with zoom factors from five to thirty.
The personal role manager organises by roles, and elastic windows make it work. You've got this.
